paper_title: Modeling social resilience: Questions, answers, open problems
original_question: How should time-window size, event-time thresholds, and temporal paths be chosen when reconstructing interaction networks from temporal observations? The question matters because these choices determine network density, topological analyses, and who can potentially influence whom in a social organization.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{O} = \{(i_k, j_k, t_k)\}_{k=1}^N$ be a finite sequence of timestamped pairwise observations among a set $V$ of agents, where $(i_k, j_k, t_k)$ records an observed interaction between $i_k, j_k \in V$ at time $t_k \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. From $\mathcal{O}$ one reconstructs an interaction network in three customary ways:

1. (Window aggregation.) Given a window size $w > 0$ and an offset $s \ge 0$, form the static graph $G_{w,s} = (V, E_{w,s})$ in which $\{i,j\} \in E_{w,s}$ iff there exists at least one observation $(i,j,t) \in \mathcal{O}$ with $t \in [s, s+w]$. The edge density and all derived topological statistics (degree distribution, clustering, components, centralities) depend on $w$ and $s$.

2. (Event-time thresholding.) Given two consecutive observations involving the same pair, only those whose inter-event gap $\Delta t$ satisfies $\Delta t \le \Delta t_{\mathrm{thr}}$ are counted as a sustained interaction edge; the resulting edge set depends on the threshold $\Delta t_{\mathrm{thr}} > 0$.

3. (Temporal paths.) A temporal path of length $\ell$ from $u$ to $v$ is a sequence $(u = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_\ell = v)$ together with times $t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_\ell$ such that each $(v_{r-1}, v_r, t_r)$ is an observation. Reachability "who can potentially influence whom" is encoded by the set $R_{\ell,\tau}(u) = \{v : \exists \text{ temporal path of length } \le \ell \text{ from } u \text{ to } v \text{ with } t_\ell - t_1 \le \tau\}$.

Problem. Provide principled, data-driven rules for choosing the parameters $w$, $s$, $\Delta t_{\mathrm{thr}}$, $\ell$, and $\tau$ from $\mathcal{O}$ so that the reconstructed networks $G_{w,s}$ and the temporal reachability sets $R_{\ell,\tau}(\cdot)$ faithfully represent the underlying interaction structure. In particular: (a) determine an optimal window size $w^*$ that balances statistical stability of topological observables against temporal resolution; (b) determine an optimal inter-event threshold $\Delta t_{\mathrm{thr}}^*$ separating genuine interactions from spurious co-occurrences; (c) determine path-length and time-horizon parameters $\ell^*, \tau^*$ for meaningful potential-influence reachability. Prove or characterize the existence, uniqueness, and consistency of such optima under a stated stochastic model of the observation process.
status_search_result: The choice of time-window size, inter-event thresholds, and temporal-path parameters in reconstructing interaction networks from temporal data remains an active methodological research question with no universally accepted optimal procedure; multiple heuristics (e.g., natural-timescale, activity-driven, motif-based) have been proposed, but no canonical solution has been established.

paper_title: Physical Layer Security in Satellite Communication: State-of-the-art and Open Problems
original_question: How can physical-layer security techniques be designed for satellite communication systems to preserve availability against denial-of-service and jamming attacks, given that satellites and satellite links can be overwhelmed by malicious traffic and can be targeted by multiple forms of jamming that distort signals and prevent correct decoding and processing, and given that any proposed method must remain feasible under the unique physical characteristics of satellite communication?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a satellite communication system modeled as follows. A legitimate transmitter T (a ground station or satellite) communicates with a legitimate receiver R over a wireless channel whose physical characteristics include: (i) very large propagation distances (LEO, MEO, or GEO orbits) producing severe path loss and propagation delays, (ii) high relative motion inducing Doppler shifts, (iii) limited on-board power and processing resources at the satellite, (iv) broad-beam coverage so that any geographic adversary within the footprint can receive and transmit on the same band, and (v) shared spectrum subject to atmospheric and ionospheric impairments. An adversary class A is allowed to mount two types of availability attacks:

(a) Denial-of-service flooding: A injects high-rate malicious traffic toward T or R such that the legitimate processing/queueing capacity is exceeded with probability at least p_DoS.

(b) Jamming: A emits interference signals (constant, pulsed, sweep, tone, protocol-aware, or smart/reactive jamming) of total average power up to P_J and arbitrary waveform structure within the system bandwidth W, with the goal of preventing correct decoding at R.

Design a physical-layer security (PLS) scheme—i.e., a transmission strategy specifying signal design, coding, beamforming, frequency/time hopping, power control, and/or admission control performed at the physical layer (without relying on cryptographic upper-layer mechanisms)—that achieves the following availability guarantee: for every admissible adversary strategy of types (a) and (b), the probability that R correctly decodes each transmitted message is at least 1 − ε, while the scheme remains implementable under the satellite physical constraints (i)–(v) (in particular, bounded on-board energy E, antenna aperture, and computational complexity polynomial in the block length).

The problem is: provide such a PLS construction together with a rigorous proof of its availability guarantee, or establish fundamental impossibility bounds (in terms of W, P_J, E, p_DoS, ε) showing the regimes in which no such scheme can exist.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction concerning PLS availability and anti-jamming in satellite communications. Recent surveys (2023–2025) continue to list anti-jamming and DoS-resilient PLS for satellite/LEO systems as open problems, with various partial schemes (e.g., spread-spectrum hopping, beam-nulling, NOMA-based jamming mitigation) proposed but no general solution under realistic satellite constraints.

paper_title: Physical Layer Security in Satellite Communication: State-of-the-art and Open Problems
original_question: How should physical-layer security for satellite systems be redesigned under stronger and more realistic threat models in which eavesdroppers are not merely passive, single-antenna, static listeners with limited resources, but may actively intercept to extract main-channel state information, possess improved antenna and signal-processing capabilities, and move dynamically with unknown locations, for example as UAV-based adversaries?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a satellite communication system in which a legitimate transmitter (e.g., a satellite or gateway) communicates with a legitimate receiver over a wireless main channel, while one or more eavesdroppers attempt to intercept the transmission. The classical wiretap-channel model assumes the eavesdropper is (i) passive (it does not transmit or otherwise influence the main channel), (ii) equipped with a single antenna and limited signal-processing resources, (iii) static with a known (or at least fixed) location, so that the legitimate parties can rely on channel state information (CSI) and location uncertainty to design beamforming, artificial-noise, secrecy-coding, or key-generation schemes that achieve a positive secrecy rate.

Formulate and analyze a physical-layer security framework for satellite links under a strictly stronger adversary model that simultaneously incorporates the following capabilities:

1. Active interception: the eavesdropper may transmit probing or pilot-contamination signals in order to extract (partial) CSI of the legitimate main channel, thereby degrading schemes that rely on CSI advantage at the legitimate receiver.
2. Enhanced hardware: the eavesdropper has multiple antennas and advanced signal-processing capability (e.g., MIMO combining, beam-steering, joint detection across multiple receive chains).
3. Mobility with unknown location: the eavesdropper is dynamic (for instance, a UAV-mounted receiver) with a position and trajectory that are unknown to the legitimate parties; only statistical or set-membership information about its location is available.

For this adversary model, determine:
(a) an appropriate information-theoretic secrecy metric (e.g., worst-case ergodic secrecy capacity or secrecy outage probability over the set of admissible eavesdropper states),
(b) achievable bounds on this metric for typical satellite channel models (line-of-sight dominated, shadowed-Rician, or hybrid satellite-terrestrial channels),
(c) explicit transmission strategies (beamforming, artificial noise, cooperative jamming, secret key generation, or coding) that achieve or approach these bounds, and
(d) sufficient conditions on the system parameters (transmit power, antenna numbers, location uncertainty set, pilot-contamination strength) under which a strictly positive secrecy rate is guaranteed.

Provide a redesign of physical-layer security for satellite systems that is provably robust against the combined effects of (1)–(3), or alternatively prove impossibility results identifying parameter regimes in which no positive secrecy rate is achievable.
category_tag: Physical-layer security under advanced adversary models
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in the area of physical-layer security for satellite communications. Existing literature primarily treats passive, single-antenna, static eavesdroppers; works addressing active pilot-contamination attacks, multi-antenna eavesdroppers, and mobile UAV eavesdroppers exist individually in terrestrial and UAV PLS contexts, but a unified, provably robust framework for satellite systems under the combined advanced threat model has not been established. Status appears open.

paper_title: Physical Layer Security in Satellite Communication: State-of-the-art and Open Problems
original_question: How can physical-layer security techniques be used to provide message integrity for satellite communication systems, so that man-in-the-middle style attacks that intercept, modify, and retransmit satellite-to-user or user-to-satellite signals can be detected reliably before corrupted information is accepted or processed?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a satellite communication system consisting of a satellite transmitter and a terrestrial user (or vice versa) communicating over a wireless channel. An adversary positioned between the two legitimate parties may carry out an integrity-violation (man-in-the-middle) attack by intercepting the transmitted signal, modifying or manipulating the carried message, and retransmitting the altered signal to the intended receiver, with the goal of disrupting service or gaining unauthorized access.

Design and analyze physical-layer security (PLS) mechanisms — that is, techniques that exploit physical characteristics of the wireless transmission (such as channel state information, channel reciprocity, propagation effects, noise statistics, hardware imperfections, or signal-level fingerprints) rather than upper-layer cryptography — that provide message integrity for such satellite links. Specifically:

1. Formulate a model of the legitimate satellite-to-user (and user-to-satellite) channel and of an active man-in-the-middle adversary capable of intercepting, modifying, and retransmitting signals.
2. Propose PLS-based message-manipulation detection schemes that allow the legitimate receiver to decide, before accepting or processing the received message, whether the signal has been tampered with in transit.
3. Establish quantitative guarantees (e.g., detection probability, false-alarm probability, and the range of adversary capabilities under which detection is reliable) for the proposed schemes in the satellite setting, accounting for the long propagation distances, large path loss, Doppler effects, and atmospheric impairments characteristic of satellite links.
status_search_result: Surveys on physical-layer security for satellite communications (2024–2025) continue to list PLS-based message-integrity / manipulation-detection mechanisms against man-in-the-middle attacks as an open research direction. Some partial approaches (e.g., exploiting atmospheric effects, PUF-based cross-layer frameworks combining DSFH at the physical layer) have been proposed for related authentication and MITM mitigation tasks, but a general PLS-based integrity-detection methodology for satellite links with quantitative guarantees has not been established.

paper_title: Physical Layer Security in Satellite Communication: State-of-the-art and Open Problems
original_question: How can machine-learning-based physical-layer security methods be adapted and validated for satellite communication systems, given that existing ML-based PLS work has been studied in other wireless settings such as device-to-device communication, cognitive networks, and non-orthogonal multiple access, but has not yet been explored for satellite scenarios or analyzed for applicability under satellite-specific operating conditions and physical characteristics?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a satellite communication system modeled as a wiretap channel in which a legitimate transmitter T (e.g., a satellite or ground station) wishes to communicate securely with a legitimate receiver R in the presence of one or more passive eavesdroppers E. The channel model must account for satellite-specific characteristics, including: (i) long propagation distances and the resulting large free-space path loss; (ii) high relative motion and Doppler shifts; (iii) line-of-sight dominated links with rain/atmospheric attenuation (e.g., shadowed-Rician or Loo fading for LEO/MEO/GEO links); (iv) wide-area beam footprints causing potential overlap between the legitimate user's region and eavesdropper regions; (v) limited on-board processing power, energy, and storage; and (vi) restricted feedback and channel-state-information acquisition.

Physical-layer security (PLS) is quantified by the secrecy capacity
   C_s = [ log_2(1 + γ_R) − log_2(1 + γ_E) ]^+ ,
where γ_R and γ_E are the instantaneous signal-to-noise ratios at R and E, and by metrics such as secrecy outage probability P_so(R_s) = Pr[C_s < R_s] and average secrecy rate E[C_s].

Machine-learning (ML)-based PLS methods (supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement-learning approaches; e.g., for beamforming design, artificial-noise injection, power allocation, relay/jammer selection, key generation from channel reciprocity, eavesdropper detection, and resource scheduling) have been developed for terrestrial settings such as device-to-device, cognitive radio, and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) networks.

Problem. Formulate, adapt, and rigorously validate ML-based PLS schemes for the satellite wiretap setting above. Specifically:
(a) Define training data models (channel datasets, eavesdropper-location priors, mobility traces) that faithfully capture the satellite environment despite the difficulty of obtaining CSI for E.
(b) Design learning architectures and loss functions whose optimization provably (or empirically) maximizes a chosen secrecy metric (secrecy rate, secrecy outage probability, or secret-key rate) subject to on-board complexity, latency, and energy constraints.
(c) Establish performance guarantees (generalization bounds, robustness to model mismatch in shadowed-Rician parameters, Doppler, and beam geometry) showing under what satellite-specific operating conditions the ML-based scheme outperforms classical PLS baselines.
(d) Provide a methodology and benchmarks to validate applicability across LEO, MEO, and GEO scenarios, including uplink, downlink, and inter-satellite links.

Determine to what extent (a)–(d) can be achieved, identifying the regimes in which ML-based PLS is provably beneficial for satellite communication and the regimes in which it fails.
status_search_result: The question is an open research direction concerning the design and validation of machine-learning-based physical-layer security techniques tailored to satellite channels. Recent surveys on PLS for satellite/non-terrestrial networks (2023–2025) continue to list ML-based PLS for satellite systems as an open problem requiring further investigation, with only preliminary studies (e.g., deep-learning beamforming for LEO secrecy) and no comprehensive validated framework.

paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
original_question: For RIS-aided sparse channel estimation in mmWave or THz settings, what pilot signals and RIS training states are optimal for sparse recovery, and what training-based capacity results follow when the channel is estimated through sparse recovery rather than standard linear estimation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a narrowband MIMO communication link aided by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS). Let the transmitter have $M_t$ antennas, the receiver have $M_r$ antennas, and the RIS have $N$ passive reflecting elements whose phase configuration at training slot $k$ is described by a diagonal matrix $\Theta_k = \mathrm{diag}(\theta_k) \in \mathbb{C}^{N\times N}$ with unit-modulus entries. Denote by $H_1 \in \mathbb{C}^{N\times M_t}$ the transmitter-to-RIS channel and by $H_2 \in \mathbb{C}^{M_r\times N}$ the RIS-to-receiver channel, so that the end-to-end (cascaded) channel for configuration $\Theta_k$ is
$$H(\Theta_k) \;=\; H_2\,\Theta_k\,H_1.$$
Assume a mmWave/THz propagation regime in which $H_1$ and $H_2$ admit sparse geometric representations
$$H_1 = A_R(\phi_1)\,\mathrm{diag}(\alpha_1)\,A_T(\psi_1)^H, \qquad H_2 = A_R(\phi_2)\,\mathrm{diag}(\alpha_2)\,A_T(\psi_2)^H,$$
where each link has only $L \ll \min(M_t,M_r,N)$ dominant paths with angles drawn from quantized dictionaries of sizes $G, H, P$ along the relevant spatial directions, and $\alpha_1,\alpha_2$ are complex gains. During training, the transmitter emits pilot symbols $\{x_k\}_{k=1}^{K}$ and the receiver observes
$$y_k = H_2\,\Theta_k\,H_1\,x_k + n_k, \qquad n_k \sim \mathcal{CN}(0,\sigma^2 I),$$
under an average pilot energy constraint $\sum_k \|x_k\|^2 \le K P_t$ and a total training budget of $K$ symbols (out of a coherence block of length $T$).

Within this model, address the following:

(a) Determine pilot signals $\{x_k\}_{k=1}^{K}$ and RIS training states $\{\Theta_k\}_{k=1}^{K}$ that are optimal (in a precise, stated sense such as minimizing worst-case or average mean-square error of the sparse-recovery estimate of $(H_1,H_2)$, or equivalently the cascaded channel, subject to the sparsity prior above) for recovery via $\ell_1$-minimization or other sparse-recovery decoders. The optimality criterion should account for the joint design of the pilot sequence and the RIS phase profiles, and should specify how restricted-isometry- or coherence-type guarantees are met with the minimum possible $K$.

(b) Derive a training-based capacity result for this RIS-aided channel in which the channel is acquired through the sparse-recovery estimator from part (a) rather than a standard linear (e.g., least-squares or LMMSE) estimator. Specifically, obtain a closed-form lower bound on the ergodic achievable rate of the form
$$R(K,P_t,T) = \frac{T-K}{T}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log_2\det\!\left(I + \rho_{\mathrm{eff}}(K,P_t)\,\widehat H \widehat H^H\right)\right],$$
where $\widehat H$ is the sparse-recovery estimate and $\rho_{\mathrm{eff}}$ accounts for residual estimation error, and optimize this bound over $K$ to characterize the optimal training length and the resulting capacity scaling in $(M_t,M_r,N,L,T,P_t)$.
status_search_result: Recent surveys and research papers on RIS-aided sparse channel estimation propose various compressive-sensing-based estimators (e.g., OMP-style algorithms with O(L log(P+GH)) pilot overhead) and pilot/RIS-phase designs, but none provide a complete characterization of jointly optimal pilots and RIS training states together with the corresponding training-based capacity. Overview papers from 2023–2024 explicitly identify this joint optimality and the associated capacity result as unresolved.

paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
original_question: For RIS-aided systems that use statistical channel state information and optimize long-term performance under infrequent RIS updates, what achievable-rate inner bounds can be derived for the ergodic-rate optimization problem, instead of relying only on outer bounds?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a single-user MIMO communication system aided by a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS). Let the transmitter, receiver, and RIS be equipped with $N_t$, $N_r$, and $M$ antennas/elements, respectively. The received signal is
$$ y = (H_d + H_2 \, \Phi \, H_1)\, x + n, $$
where $H_d \in \mathbb{C}^{N_r \times N_t}$ is the direct channel, $H_1 \in \mathbb{C}^{M \times N_t}$ and $H_2 \in \mathbb{C}^{N_r \times M}$ are the transmitter–RIS and RIS–receiver channels, $\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(e^{j\theta_1},\dots,e^{j\theta_M})$ is the diagonal RIS phase-shift matrix with $\theta_m \in [0,2\pi)$, $x$ is the transmit signal with covariance $Q\succeq 0$, $\mathrm{tr}(Q)\le P$, and $n\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,\sigma^2 I)$.

Assume that the channels $H_d, H_1, H_2$ are random with a known joint distribution (statistical CSI), and that the RIS configuration $\Phi$ together with the input covariance $Q$ are chosen as functions of this distribution only (i.e., they are held fixed over the coherence horizon during which the instantaneous channels vary). Define the ergodic rate
$$ R(\Phi, Q) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[ \log\det\!\left( I + \tfrac{1}{\sigma^2}(H_d + H_2 \Phi H_1) Q (H_d + H_2 \Phi H_1)^H \right) \right], $$
with the ergodic-rate optimization problem
$$ R^\star = \sup_{\Phi,\, Q:\ \mathrm{tr}(Q)\le P} R(\Phi, Q). $$

Problem. Derive a closed-form achievable-rate inner bound $\underline{R}(\Phi,Q)$, satisfying $\underline{R}(\Phi,Q) \le R(\Phi,Q)$ for all feasible $(\Phi,Q)$, that depends only on the channel statistics (e.g., covariance matrices, line-of-sight components, Rician factors) and that can be used as a tractable surrogate objective for optimizing the long-term RIS configuration $\Phi$ and input covariance $Q$ when only statistical CSI is available. The bound should be tight enough to provide a meaningful guarantee on the achievable ergodic rate, and the resulting optimization should be amenable to practical algorithms.
status_search_result: Since 2023, several works have derived closed-form approximations and lower bounds on the ergodic rate of RIS-aided systems under statistical CSI using tools such as Jensen's inequality, majorization theory, and large-system/asymptotic analysis, including for single-RIS MISO, double-RIS MIMO with spatial correlation, and stacked intelligent metasurfaces. Many derive asymptotic or approximate ergodic-rate expressions rather than fully rigorous inner bounds, and general tight inner bounds for arbitrary correlated MIMO settings remain an active topic of research.

paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
original_question: Can an RIS channel model be derived that keeps the end-to-end channel in a factored form GΦH, while still capturing mutual impedances and coupling by allowing the RIS matrix Φ to become a possibly non-diagonal function of circuit parameters, and can a practical channel-estimation method be built for that model?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a wireless communication link assisted by a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS) consisting of N reconfigurable scattering elements. Let H ∈ ℂ^{N×M} denote the channel from an M-antenna transmitter to the RIS elements, and let G ∈ ℂ^{K×N} denote the channel from the RIS elements to a K-antenna receiver. In the standard (idealized) model, the end-to-end channel from transmitter to receiver is written in the factored form

  H_e2e = G Φ H,

where Φ ∈ ℂ^{N×N} is a diagonal matrix whose n-th diagonal entry encodes the reflection coefficient applied by the n-th RIS element, and is parameterized by tunable circuit parameters (e.g. varactor capacitances or PIN-diode states). This idealization ignores electromagnetic mutual impedances and mutual coupling among the densely packed RIS elements.

Let S ∈ ℂ^{N×N} denote the (frequency-dependent, geometry-determined) mutual scattering/impedance matrix of the RIS array, and let Γ(c) ∈ ℂ^{N×N} be a diagonal matrix of element loads parameterized by the vector c ∈ ℝ^N (or ℂ^N) of tunable circuit parameters. A physically consistent multiport-network model leads to an RIS response matrix

  Φ(c) = f(S, Γ(c)),

which in general is non-diagonal and depends jointly on S and on the circuit parameters c.

The problem has two parts:

(1) Derivation. Determine whether there exists a channel model that (a) retains the strictly factored form H_e2e = G Φ(c) H, with G and H independent of c and depending only on the propagation environment between the transmitter / receiver and the RIS, and (b) faithfully captures the mutual-impedance and mutual-coupling effects of the RIS array through a (possibly non-diagonal) matrix Φ(c) that is an explicit function of the circuit parameters c and of the coupling/impedance data of the array.

(2) Estimation. Assuming such a factored model exists, design a practical pilot-based channel-estimation procedure that, from observed input–output measurements taken under a set of training configurations {c_t}, recovers the parameters of G and H (and, if needed, of the coupling structure) with computational and pilot overhead that scales favorably in N, K, and M.
category_tag: RIS channel estimation with mutual coupling
status_search_result: Several works (2023–2025) develop physics-consistent multiport-network and scattering-parameter models for RIS in which the RIS response matrix becomes non-diagonal due to mutual coupling, and propose mutual-coupling-aware channel-estimation algorithms (e.g., compressed-sensing formulations, two-stage MC-unaware/MC-aware estimation, and BD-RIS modeling). These results provide candidate factored or near-factored representations and practical estimators, but a fully general factored model G Φ(c) H that exactly captures arbitrary mutual coupling while admitting a scalable estimator is still under active investigation, so the problem is best regarded as partially solved.

paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
original_question: If RIS elements cannot be perfectly deactivated in practice, how does imperfect deactivation change the accuracy and robustness of channel-estimation methods that assume complete absorption, complete transmission, or complete removal of RIS reflections?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a wireless communication system equipped with a Reconfigurable Intelligent Surface (RIS) consisting of N passive reflecting elements. Let the cascaded channel between a single-antenna transmitter and a single-antenna receiver via the RIS be modeled as

 y = (h_d + g^T diag(theta) f) x + n,

where h_d ∈ C is the direct (non-RIS) channel, f ∈ C^N is the transmitter-to-RIS channel, g ∈ C^N is the RIS-to-receiver channel, x is the transmitted pilot, n ~ CN(0, sigma^2) is additive Gaussian noise, and theta = (theta_1, ..., theta_N)^T ∈ C^N collects the reflection coefficients of the RIS elements. In an ideal model, each element n can be configured in one of three "deactivated" modes:
 (i) complete absorption: theta_n = 0,
 (ii) complete transmission (pass-through): the element forwards x with unit gain and no phase shift to the receiver via the direct path,
 (iii) complete removal of reflection: the element contributes nothing to g^T diag(theta) f.

Many channel-estimation schemes for f and g (or for the cascaded coefficients g_n f_n) rely on switching subsets of RIS elements into one of these idealized deactivated states during pilot transmissions in order to isolate or cancel contributions. In practice, however, an element configured to be "deactivated" still produces a residual reflection coefficient theta_n^res, which can be modeled as a random variable on C with |theta_n^res| ≤ epsilon for some leakage parameter epsilon > 0 (or, more generally, with a specified distribution centered near 0 but with nonzero mean and variance).

Problem. Develop a quantitative analysis of how this imperfect deactivation affects channel estimation of (h_d, f, g). Specifically:

(a) For a given estimator E (e.g., least squares, LMMSE, or compressed-sensing-based) that assumes ideal deactivation, derive the bias and mean-square error of the resulting estimates of h_d, f, and g as functions of the leakage statistics of {theta_n^res} and of N.

(b) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the leakage distribution (in terms of epsilon, mean, and covariance) under which the estimator E remains consistent as the pilot length and/or N tend to infinity.

paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
original_question: Do the wideband remedies proposed in the reflectarray literature, such as true time-delay lines or multiple resonance elements, actually transfer to RIS-aided communication systems, and under what operating assumptions would they preserve useful beamforming behavior across the communication band?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) consisting of $N$ passive reflecting elements, each capable of imposing a (possibly frequency-dependent) reflection coefficient on impinging electromagnetic waves. Suppose the RIS assists a communication link operating over a wideband channel of carrier frequency $f_c$ and bandwidth $B$, where $B/f_c$ is not negligible (so that beam-squint phenomena are non-trivial).

In the reflectarray literature, two principal techniques have been proposed to widen the operating bandwidth of passive reflecting surfaces:
(a) coupling each radiating element to a true time-delay (TTD) line, so that the element imposes a frequency-linear phase response $\phi_n(f) = -2\pi f \tau_n$ for some controllable delay $\tau_n$; and
(b) coupling multiple resonance elements (e.g., stacked patches or multi-resonator unit cells), so that the element's phase response remains approximately linear, or at least controlled, across a broad band.

Formulate and resolve the following questions:

1. Under what assumptions on the RIS element architecture, the propagation geometry (far-field versus near-field, planar wave assumption), the channel model (line-of-sight, multipath, frequency selectivity), and the achievable delay/phase control resolution do the wideband remedies (a) and (b) from the reflectarray literature transfer to RIS-aided communication systems while preserving useful beamforming gain (e.g., array gain $\geq (1-\epsilon) N^2$ for prescribed $\epsilon>0$) uniformly across the band $[f_c - B/2,\, f_c + B/2]$?

2. Quantify, as a function of $N$, $B/f_c$, the steering angle, and the delay resolution, the worst-case beamforming loss and the residual beam-squint after application of (a) or (b), and identify operating regimes in which these techniques are provably effective for wideband RIS communication.
status_search_result: Recent works (2022–2024) have begun adapting reflectarray wideband remedies to RIS. In particular, time-delay-unit-based architectures coupled with element-grouping strategies have been shown to mitigate beam squint in RIS-aided communications, and hybrid TTD/phase-shifter schemes plus space–frequency-transform-based phase designs have been proposed for wideband and near-field RIS beamforming. The general question of when reflectarray-style wideband techniques transfer to RIS with provable uniform beamforming gain is therefore partially addressed but not fully resolved, especially for multi-resonance passive RIS elements and near-field/multipath regimes.

paper_title: Concrete examples of the rate of convergence of Chernoff approximations: numerical results for the heat semigroup and open questions on them (with appendix: full list of pictures and Python code)
context_brief: Chernoff rates below known regularity hypotheses
original_question: Let UC_b(R) be the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous real functions with the sup norm, and let Lf=f'' generate the heat semigroup e^{tL}. Existing rate theorems for Chernoff approximations require smoothness and domain conditions, such as membership in powers of D(L). If those conditions fail, for example when an initial condition f is differentiable only once but not twice and f' is Hölder continuous with exponent 1/2, what is the asymptotic convergence rate of C(t/n)^n f to e^{tL}f as n tends to infinity? More generally, how does the rate depend on the smoothness of f and on whether the Chernoff function C has first-order or higher-order Chernoff tangency to L when f is not in the regularity class covered by the known theorem?
self_contained_problem:
Let $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ denote the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ equipped with the supremum norm $\|f\|_\infty=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|f(x)|$. Let $L$ be the closed operator on $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ defined by $Lf=f''$ on its natural domain $D(L)=\{f\in UC_b(\mathbb{R}): f''\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})\}$. Then $L$ generates the heat semigroup $(e^{tL})_{t\ge 0}$ on $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$, given by 
$$(e^{tL}f)(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi t}}\int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-(x-y)^2/(4t)}f(y)\,dy,\qquad t>0.$$

A strongly continuous family of bounded linear operators $(C(t))_{t\ge 0}$ on $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ with $C(0)=I$ is called a Chernoff function of order $k\ge 1$ tangent to $L$ if for every $f\in D(L^k)$,
$$C(t)f = f + tLf + \tfrac{t^2}{2!}L^2 f + \cdots + \tfrac{t^k}{k!}L^k f + o(t^k)\quad\text{as }t\to 0^+,$$
together with the standard Chernoff hypotheses ensuring $C(t/n)^n f\to e^{tL}f$ in $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ for every $f\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ as $n\to\infty$.

Known rate theorems guarantee, for fixed $t>0$ and $f\in D(L^k)$, that
$$\|C(t/n)^n f - e^{tL}f\|_\infty = O(n^{-k})\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.$$

Now consider $f\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ such that $f$ is once continuously differentiable with $f'\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ Hölder continuous of exponent $1/2$, but $f\notin D(L)$ (i.e.\ $f''$ does not exist as an element of $UC_b(\mathbb{R})$).

(a) Determine the asymptotic rate of convergence of $\|C(t/n)^n f - e^{tL}f\|_\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, for $t>0$ fixed, when $C$ has first-order Chernoff tangency to $L$.

(b) More generally, for $f\in UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ whose smoothness is described by a Hölder/Sobolev-type modulus weaker than membership in $D(L^k)$, determine how the asymptotic rate of $\|C(t/n)^n f - e^{tL}f\|_\infty$ depends jointly on the smoothness of $f$ and on the order of Chernoff tangency $k$ of $C$ to $L$.
status_search_result: The question of the convergence rate of Chernoff approximations to the heat semigroup for initial conditions outside the standard regularity classes (e.g., $f\notin D(L)$ with only Hölder-regular first derivative) appears still open. Recent works on Chernoff approximations (e.g., upper/lower estimates in the Chernoff product formula, 2024 Israel J. Math.; convergence rates for convex monotone semigroups, 2025) provide rates under regularity assumptions but do not settle the precise asymptotic rate in the low-regularity regime described.

paper_title: Concrete examples of the rate of convergence of Chernoff approximations: numerical results for the heat semigroup and open questions on them (with appendix: full list of pictures and Python code)
context_brief: Quality of log-log linear error fits
original_question: For the heat equation u_t(t,x)=u_xx(t,x) on the real line, work in the Banach space UC_b(R) of bounded uniformly continuous real functions with the sup norm. Let Lf=f'' generate the heat semigroup e^{tL}. For t=1/2, compare the exact solution e^{tL}u0 with Chernoff products G(t/n)^n u0 and S(t/n)^n u0, where G is first-order Chernoff tangent to L and S is second-order Chernoff tangent to L. Write d_n^G=||e^{tL}u0-G(t/n)^n u0|| and d_n^S=||e^{tL}u0-S(t/n)^n u0||, and estimate log d_n approximately as alpha log n plus beta, where alpha is the order of decreasing error and beta is the free term. Why does the log-log relationship between the approximation error and n have very different quality of linear fit for different initial conditions? In particular, what theoretical mechanism makes the fit essentially perfect for u0(x)=sin x and u0(x)=cos x and also good for the nonsmooth initial condition u0(x)=|sin x|^(1/4), while the smooth initial condition u0(x)=exp(-x^4) gives a noticeably poorer fit, contrary to a naive expectation that higher smoothness should improve the fit?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F = UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ denote the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous functions $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with the sup norm $\|f\| = \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} |f(x)|$. Consider the heat equation $u_t(t,x) = u_{xx}(t,x)$ on $\mathbb{R}$, whose solution defines the heat semigroup $(e^{tL})_{t\ge 0}$ in $F$ generated by $Lf = f''$.

Define the bounded linear operators on $F$
$$ (G(t)f)(x) = \tfrac{1}{2} f(x) + \tfrac{1}{4} f(x+2\sqrt{t}) + \tfrac{1}{4} f(x-2\sqrt{t}), $$
$$ (S(t)f)(x) = \tfrac{2}{3} f(x) + \tfrac{1}{6} f(x+\sqrt{6t}) + \tfrac{1}{6} f(x-\sqrt{6t}). $$
Then $G$ is Chernoff-tangent to $L$ of first order, and $S$ is Chernoff-tangent to $L$ of second order, so by Chernoff's theorem, for every $t>0$ and every $u_0\in F$,
$$ d_n^G := \|e^{tL}u_0 - G(t/n)^n u_0\| \to 0, \qquad d_n^S := \|e^{tL}u_0 - S(t/n)^n u_0\| \to 0 \quad (n\to\infty). $$
Fix $t = 1/2$. Empirically one observes a log-log linear relation $\ln d_n \approx \alpha \ln n + \beta$, where $\alpha$ is called the order of the decreasing error and $\beta$ the free term.

Numerical computation shows:
- For $u_0(x) = \sin x$ and $u_0(x) = \cos x$, the linear fit $\ln d_n$ vs $\ln n$ is essentially perfect.
- For the nonsmooth $u_0(x) = |\sin x|^{1/4}$, the linear fit is good.
- For the smooth $u_0(x) = \exp(-x^4)$, the linear fit is noticeably poorer, contrary to the naive expectation that higher regularity should improve the fit.

Provide a theoretical explanation: identify a mechanism (in terms of the structure of $G$, $S$, the heat semigroup, and the initial datum) that determines the quality of the log-log linear fit of $d_n^G$ and $d_n^S$ as functions of $n$, and that explains why the eigenfunctions $\sin x, \cos x$ produce a perfect fit, why $|\sin x|^{1/4}$ still produces a good fit, while $\exp(-x^4)$ produces a poorer one.
status_search_result: The originating work explicitly lists this phenomenon among effects observed numerically but not theoretically explained, and frames it as an open question. No subsequent published resolution was located.

paper_title: Concrete examples of the rate of convergence of Chernoff approximations: numerical results for the heat semigroup and open questions on them (with appendix: full list of pictures and Python code)
context_brief: Opposite behavior of error order and free term
original_question: For the heat equation u_t(t,x)=u_xx(t,x) on the real line, work in the Banach space UC_b(R) of bounded uniformly continuous real functions with the sup norm. Let Lf=f'' generate the heat semigroup e^{tL}. For t=1/2, compare the exact solution e^{tL}u0 with Chernoff products G(t/n)^n u0 and S(t/n)^n u0, where G is first-order Chernoff tangent to L and S is second-order Chernoff tangent to L. Write d_n^G=||e^{tL}u0-G(t/n)^n u0|| and d_n^S=||e^{tL}u0-S(t/n)^n u0||, and estimate log d_n approximately as alpha log n plus beta, where alpha is the order of decreasing error and beta is the free term. Why does the second-order Chernoff function S consistently improve the order of decreasing error, in the sense that alpha_S is smaller than alpha_G, while usually having a worse free term, in the sense that beta_S is larger than beta_G? What theory explains this opposite behavior between the asymptotic power alpha and the multiplicative prefactor exp(beta), including the noted exceptions u0(x)=sin x and u0(x)=exp(-|x|^(5/2))?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F = UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ denote the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous real-valued functions on $\mathbb{R}$, equipped with the supremum norm $\|f\| = \sup_{x \in \mathbb{R}} |f(x)|$. Let $L$ be the operator $Lf = f''$ on its natural domain, and let $(e^{tL})_{t \ge 0}$ be the heat semigroup, so that $u(t,\cdot) = e^{tL}u_0$ solves the Cauchy problem $u_t = u_{xx}$, $u(0,\cdot) = u_0$.

Define two families of bounded linear operators on $F$ by
$$ (G(t)f)(x) = \tfrac{1}{2} f(x) + \tfrac{1}{4} f(x + 2\sqrt{t}) + \tfrac{1}{4} f(x - 2\sqrt{t}), $$
$$ (S(t)f)(x) = \tfrac{2}{3} f(x) + \tfrac{1}{6} f(x + \sqrt{6t}) + \tfrac{1}{6} f(x - \sqrt{6t}). $$
The family $G$ is a Chernoff function tangent to $L$ of order $1$, while $S$ is tangent to $L$ of order $2$ (i.e., $G(t) = I + tL + o(t)$ and $S(t) = I + tL + \tfrac{t^2}{2}L^2 + o(t^2)$ in a strong sense on a suitable core). Chernoff's theorem implies that for each $u_0 \in F$ and each fixed $t > 0$,
$$ d_n^G := \|e^{tL}u_0 - G(t/n)^n u_0\| \to 0, \qquad d_n^S := \|e^{tL}u_0 - S(t/n)^n u_0\| \to 0 $$
as $n \to \infty$.

Fix $t = 1/2$. For a broad family of initial data $u_0$ (including the cases $u_0(x) = \sin x$ and $u_0(x) = \exp(-|x|^{5/2})$ as distinguished examples), one observes numerically a power-law behavior
$$ \ln d_n^G \approx \alpha_G \ln n + \beta_G, \qquad \ln d_n^S \approx \alpha_S \ln n + \beta_S, $$
with $\alpha_G, \alpha_S < 0$ called the orders of decreasing error and $\beta_G, \beta_S$ the free terms.

Provide a rigorous theoretical explanation for the empirically observed inequality $\alpha_S < \alpha_G$ (so that the second-order Chernoff function strictly improves the exponent in the convergence rate) occurring simultaneously with the inequality $\beta_S > \beta_G$ (so that the multiplicative prefactor $e^{\beta_S}$ is worse than $e^{\beta_G}$). Identify in particular which structural properties of $u_0$ govern $(\alpha_G,\beta_G,\alpha_S,\beta_S)$, and account for the exceptional behavior at $u_0(x) = \sin x$ and $u_0(x) = \exp(-|x|^{5/2})$.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem about explaining numerical observations on rate-of-convergence exponents and prefactors for first- and second-order Chernoff approximations to the heat semigroup. Recent works (e.g., Galkin–Remizov, Israel J. Math. 2024, on upper and lower estimates for rates of convergence in Chernoff product formulas) establish that higher-order Chernoff tangency yields improved power-law rate $O(n^{-k})$, which is consistent with $\alpha_S < \alpha_G$, but the literature does not appear to provide a quantitative theory explaining the simultaneously worse prefactor $e^{\beta_S} > e^{\beta_G}$ or the noted exceptions. No publication was found that resolves this specific opposite-behavior phenomenon.

context_brief: Error behavior for infinitely smooth data
original_question: For the heat equation u_t(t,x)=u_xx(t,x) on the real line, work in the Banach space UC_b(R) of bounded uniformly continuous real functions with the sup norm. Let Lf=f'' generate the heat semigroup e^{tL}. For t=1/2, compare the exact solution e^{tL}u0 with Chernoff products G(t/n)^n u0 and S(t/n)^n u0, where G is first-order Chernoff tangent to L and S is second-order Chernoff tangent to L. Write d_n^G=||e^{tL}u0-G(t/n)^n u0|| and d_n^S=||e^{tL}u0-S(t/n)^n u0||, and estimate log d_n approximately as alpha log n plus beta, where alpha is the order of decreasing error and beta is the free term. Among infinitely smooth initial conditions, what properties beyond infinite differentiability determine the observed order of decreasing error for Chernoff approximation of the heat semigroup? In particular, why do u0(x)=sin x, u0(x)=exp(-x^2), u0(x)=exp(-x^4), and u0(x)=exp(-x^6) produce substantially different pairs of estimated orders (alpha_G, alpha_S), including the case exp(-x^6) where the first-order and second-order Chernoff functions have nearly the same observed order?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F = UC_b(\mathbb{R})$ be the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous real-valued functions on $\mathbb{R}$ equipped with the sup-norm $\|f\| = \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} |f(x)|$. Let $L\colon\mathrm{Dom}(L)\subset F\to F$ be the operator $Lf=f''$, which generates the heat $C_0$-semigroup $(e^{tL})_{t\ge 0}$ on $F$, namely the semigroup solving the Cauchy problem $u_t(t,x)=u_{xx}(t,x)$, $u(0,\cdot)=u_0$.

Define two families of bounded linear operators on $F$ by
$$(G(t)f)(x) = \tfrac{1}{2} f(x) + \tfrac{1}{4} f(x+2\sqrt{t}) + \tfrac{1}{4} f(x-2\sqrt{t}),$$
$$(S(t)f)(x) = \tfrac{2}{3} f(x) + \tfrac{1}{6} f(x+\sqrt{6t}) + \tfrac{1}{6} f(x-\sqrt{6t}).$$
These are first-order, respectively second-order, Chernoff-tangent to $L$, meaning $G(0)=S(0)=\mathrm{Id}$ and the Taylor expansions of $G(t)f$ and $S(t)f$ at $t=0$ match those of $e^{tL}f$ up to the corresponding order on sufficiently smooth $f$. By Chernoff's theorem, for every $u_0\in F$ and every $t>0$,
$$d_n^G(u_0,t) := \|e^{tL}u_0 - G(t/n)^n u_0\| \to 0, \qquad d_n^S(u_0,t) := \|e^{tL}u_0 - S(t/n)^n u_0\| \to 0$$
as $n\to\infty$. Fix $t=1/2$ and, for a given $u_0$, define the empirical orders $\alpha_G(u_0), \alpha_S(u_0)$ and free terms $\beta_G(u_0), \beta_S(u_0)$ by the linear fits
$$\ln d_n^G \approx \alpha_G \ln n + \beta_G, \qquad \ln d_n^S \approx \alpha_S \ln n + \beta_S.$$

Numerical experiments with the four infinitely differentiable initial conditions
$$u_0(x)=\sin x,\quad u_0(x)=e^{-x^2},\quad u_0(x)=e^{-x^4},\quad u_0(x)=e^{-x^6}$$
yield substantially different pairs $(\alpha_G, \alpha_S)$, including the phenomenon that for $u_0(x)=e^{-x^6}$ the first-order and second-order Chernoff approximations exhibit essentially the same observed order.

Problem: Identify a property (or set of properties) of an initial condition $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})\cap F$, beyond mere $C^\infty$-smoothness, that determines the observed orders $\alpha_G(u_0)$ and $\alpha_S(u_0)$ of decreasing error in the Chernoff approximations of the heat semigroup, and explain in particular why $\sin x$, $e^{-x^2}$, $e^{-x^4}$, and $e^{-x^6}$ produce distinct pairs $(\alpha_G,\alpha_S)$, and why for $e^{-x^6}$ one has $\alpha_G\approx \alpha_S$.
status_search_result: The question is explicitly posed as an open numerical/empirical problem about how features of smooth initial data (beyond $C^\infty$-regularity) control the order of convergence of first- and second-order Chernoff approximations to the heat semigroup. Related rate-of-convergence results exist (e.g. upper/lower estimates in the Chernoff product formula, Galkin–Remizov style speed-of-convergence results for the heat and transport equations), but no source identifies the property determining the empirical $(\alpha_G,\alpha_S)$ for the listed Gaussian-type smooth initial conditions. paper_title: An Overview of Compact Star Populations and Some of Its Open Problems
original_question: Do neutron-star magnetic fields genuinely decay over astrophysical timescales, and if so do they fade almost completely within about 10^6 years or instead decay only partially to a persistent 'bottom field' that remains substantial even in very old systems such as black widows?
self_contained_problem:
A neutron star is a compact stellar remnant endowed with a magnetic field whose surface strength B can be inferred from pulsar timing (via the spin period P and its derivative). Observations of neutron star populations across a wide range of ages (from young pulsars at ages ~10^3–10^6 yr to recycled millisecond pulsars and "black widow" systems with characteristic ages ≳10^9 yr) raise the following question about the long-term evolution of B(t):

Determine whether the magnetic field of an isolated or binary neutron star genuinely decays as a function of age on astrophysical timescales, and if so characterize the asymptotic behavior. Specifically, decide between the following competing scenarios and identify the physical mechanism responsible:

(a) B(t) decays almost completely on a timescale of order 10^6 years, so that very old neutron stars retain only negligible magnetic fields;

(b) B(t) decays only partially toward a finite, non-zero "bottom field" B_min > 0 that persists even in systems with evolution times ≳10^9 yr, as suggested by inferred field strengths of black-widow pulsars and other very old recycled systems.

Provide a quantitative model B(t) (including dependence on accretion history, crustal impurity, and thermal evolution) that is consistent with the observed distribution of magnetic field strengths in the full neutron-star population, and either establish the existence and value of B_min or rule it out.
status_search_result: The question of whether neutron-star magnetic fields decay completely or only partially to a non-zero "bottom field" remains an active open problem. Studies of black-widow pulsars indicate the field does not fall below a minimum value despite very long evolution times, but the underlying mechanism (linked to anomalies in neutron-star cooling models and the role of crustal impurity) is not yet established.

paper_title: An Overview of Compact Star Populations and Some of Its Open Problems
original_question: Are the recently discovered ultra-slow magnetars and other very long-period neutron-star candidates simply older evolutionary stages of magnetars that have cooled and spun down to extremely long periods, or are they a distinct population, possibly closer in nature to RRATs than to standard magnetar evolution?
self_contained_problem:
Consider isolated neutron stars exhibiting rotational periods far longer than those of the canonical magnetar population (periods of minutes to hours), referred to here as ultra-slow magnetars or ultra-long period transients, together with the class of Rotating Radio Transients (RRATs), which are neutron stars detected only via sporadic, short-duration radio bursts rather than persistent pulsations.

Standard magnetar evolution predicts that strongly magnetized neutron stars are born with periods of order 1 s and, through magnetic dipole braking enhanced by their ultra-strong fields (B ~ 10^14–10^15 G), spin down while their interiors cool over time.

Determine whether the following alternative is correct:

(a) The recently observed ultra-slow magnetars and other very-long-period neutron-star candidates are simply older, cooled and spun-down evolutionary descendants of ordinary magnetars; or

(b) They constitute a physically distinct population whose properties (e.g., quiescent X-ray luminosity, radio emission behavior, magnetothermal evolution) are more closely related to RRATs than to the standard magnetar evolutionary track.

Specifically, identify whether there exists a real physical distinction between RRATs and ultra-slow magnetars, and characterize the evolutionary channel(s) that produce neutron stars with periods of minutes to hours.
status_search_result: The question remains open as of 2025–2026. Recent theoretical work (e.g., "Late-blooming magnetars" model, May 2025) proposes that ultra-long period transients could be magnetars that remained dormant during an initial cooling epoch before crustal Hall-driven activity began, but the connection to RRATs and the precise evolutionary status of ultra-slow magnetars is still actively debated. Other modeling of magnetar spin evolution suggests magnetars are unlikely to evolve into RRATs, favoring an evolutionary link instead with X-ray dim isolated neutron stars. No consensus has been established.

paper_title: The cosmological constant, dark matter, supersymmetry, and other unsolved problems from a fresh perspective
original_question: What is the physical origin of Yukawa couplings in a fundamental theory that aims to extend the standard models of particle physics and cosmology?
self_contained_problem:
In the Standard Model of particle physics, the masses of the quarks and charged leptons, together with the CKM mixing matrix (and, in extensions, the PMNS matrix for neutrinos), are encoded in dimensionless Yukawa coupling matrices Y_u, Y_d, Y_e (and Y_ν) that appear in the gauge-invariant Lagrangian terms
  L_Yuk = − (Y_u)_{ij}  ar Q_{L,i} 	ilde H u_{R,j} − (Y_d)_{ij}  ar Q_{L,i} H d_{R,j} − (Y_e)_{ij}  ar L_{L,i} H e_{R,j} + h.c.,
where H is the Higgs doublet, 	ilde H = iσ_2 H^*, Q_L and L_L are the left-handed quark and lepton doublets, and u_R, d_R, e_R are the right-handed singlets, with i,j ∈ {1,2,3} flavor indices. Within the Standard Model these Yukawa matrices are free parameters: their numerical values (which span roughly twelve orders of magnitude from the electron Yukawa ~10^{-6} to the top Yukawa ~1) and their mixing structure are fitted to experiment rather than derived.

Problem: Construct a fundamental theory, extending the Standard Models of particle physics and cosmology, in which the Yukawa coupling matrices Y_u, Y_d, Y_e (and Y_ν) are not free parameters but are determined from first principles. Specifically, identify the physical/mathematical origin of these couplings — for instance from symmetry principles, geometric or topological data of an underlying space, dynamical (e.g., fixed-point) considerations, or other structural inputs — and show that the resulting predictions reproduce the observed fermion masses and mixing angles.
status_search_result: The origin of Yukawa couplings (the "flavor puzzle") is a long-standing open problem in fundamental physics. Many proposals exist — Froggatt–Nielsen mechanisms, extra-dimensional/string-theoretic constructions, modular flavor symmetries, GUT relations, anarchy hypotheses, etc. — but no derivation has been broadly accepted as explaining the observed pattern of fermion masses and mixings from first principles.

original_question: What is the nature of dark energy in a framework that seeks to extend the standard models of particle physics and cosmology?
self_contained_problem: In the framework of modern theoretical physics, the standard model of particle physics describes the known elementary particles and their interactions via the gauge group SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1), while the standard model of cosmology (ΛCDM) describes the large-scale evolution of the universe via Einstein's field equations with a cosmological constant Λ and a cold dark matter component. Observations indicate that approximately 70% of the energy density of the present universe behaves as a component with negative pressure driving accelerated cosmic expansion, conventionally modeled either by a cosmological constant Λ in Einstein's equations or by a dynamical field (e.g. quintessence). Identify the fundamental physical nature and theoretical origin of this dark energy component, and provide a derivation, within an extension of the standard models of particle physics and cosmology, that explains both its existence and its observed energy density scale.
status_search_result: The nature of dark energy remains one of the major unsolved problems of fundamental physics and cosmology. No widely accepted derivation of its origin or magnitude exists; ongoing experimental programs (DESI, Euclid) and theoretical proposals continue, with recent DESI results (2024–2025) suggesting possible evolution of the dark energy equation of state but no settled theoretical explanation.

paper_title: The cosmological constant, dark matter, supersymmetry, and other unsolved problems from a fresh perspective
original_question: What new mechanism for CP violation can explain the prevalence of matter over antimatter in the current universe?
self_contained_problem:
In the Standard Model of particle physics, the combined charge-conjugation and parity symmetry (CP) is violated in the quark sector through a single complex phase in the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa mixing matrix. The amount of CP violation predicted by this mechanism is known to be many orders of magnitude too small to account for the observed cosmological baryon asymmetry, i.e., the dominance of matter over antimatter in the present-day universe (with baryon-to-photon ratio of order 10^{-10}). Sakharov's conditions state that to dynamically generate such an asymmetry from a symmetric initial state one needs (i) baryon number violation, (ii) C and CP violation, and (iii) a departure from thermal equilibrium.

Problem: Propose and analyze a new mechanism of CP violation — beyond the Cabibbo–Kobayashi–Maskawa phase of the Standard Model — that, together with appropriate baryon-number-violating interactions and out-of-equilibrium dynamics in the early universe, quantitatively reproduces the observed matter–antimatter asymmetry of the present universe. Specify the underlying field-theoretic model, identify the new CP-violating phases or operators, and compute the resulting baryon-to-entropy ratio, demonstrating that it agrees with the observed value while remaining consistent with current experimental bounds (electric dipole moments, flavor-changing neutral currents, collider searches, etc.).
status_search_result: Generating the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe requires CP violation beyond that of the Standard Model, and identifying the actual mechanism (e.g., electroweak baryogenesis, leptogenesis, Affleck–Dine, etc.) is a long-standing open problem in particle physics and cosmology. No experimentally confirmed mechanism is currently known as of 2026.

original_question: What determines the values of the fundamental gauge coupling constant g0 and the gravitational coupling constant G, given that this would require a detailed understanding of very complex vacuum fields after multiple symmetry breakings at various energy scales?
self_contained_problem: Within a unified field-theoretic framework in which all known interactions arise from a single underlying theory with a hierarchy of spontaneous symmetry breakings at successively lower energy scales, determine, from first principles, the numerical values of the fundamental dimensionless gauge coupling constant g_0 (the unified gauge coupling defined at the highest unification scale, before any symmetry breaking) and the gravitational coupling constant G (Newton's constant, equivalently expressed as the dimensionless ratio G m_p^2/ħc using the proton mass m_p, or as the inverse square of the Planck mass). context_brief: Control under mean-field and graph limits
original_question: When a multi-agent system is represented across several limiting descriptions, including microscopic dynamics, mean-field limits, graph limits, and embedding-based representations, how do optimal control problems behave under those limiting procedures? In particular, when passing between these scales, what properties of the control problem are preserved, changed, or lost?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a multi-agent system whose state can be described at several scales and through several limiting procedures:

1. A microscopic description by a system of N coupled ordinary differential equations
   x_i'(t) = F(x_i(t), (x_j(t))_{j=1..N}, u_i(t)),  i = 1,...,N,
   where x_i(t) ∈ R^d is the state of agent i and u_i ∈ U_ad is a control taking values in a fixed admissible control set;

2. A mean-field description, in which as N → ∞ the empirical measure μ^N_t = (1/N) Σ δ_{x_i(t)} converges to a probability measure μ_t solving a continuity/Vlasov-type PDE
   ∂_t μ_t + div(V[μ_t, ν_t] μ_t) = 0,
   driven by a measure-valued control ν_t;

3. A graph-limit (graphon) description, in which the interaction weights w_{ij}^N converge to a graphon W: [0,1]^2 → R and the agent population converges to a continuum of agents indexed by α ∈ [0,1] whose state x(t,α) evolves according to an integro-differential equation involving W;

4. An embedding-based description, in which agents are represented as points/measures in a common Hilbert or Wasserstein space, and the dynamics and controls are formulated in this embedding.

Associated to each level is an optimal control problem of minimizing a cost functional J of the form
   J = ∫_0^T L(state, control) dt + Φ(state(T))
   subject to the corresponding dynamics, over admissible controls in U_ad.

Problem. Develop a rigorous theory of optimal control under these limiting procedures. Specifically:

(a) Identify conditions on F, L, Φ, the interaction kernels, and the admissible controls under which the value functions and optimal controls of the microscopic problems converge (e.g., in the sense of Γ-convergence) to those of the mean-field, graphon, and embedding-based control problems, and characterize the limit problems explicitly.

(b) Determine which structural properties of the control problem (existence of optimizers, Pontryagin-type optimality conditions, dynamic programming / Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations, controllability, stability of optimal trajectories, regularity of the value function) are preserved when passing between any two of these descriptions, and which are altered or lost.

(c) Establish the commutativity (or quantify the failure of commutativity) of the diagram whose vertices are the four control problems and whose edges are the mean-field limit, the graph limit, and the embedding maps.
status_search_result: Partial results exist: Γ-convergence of finite-agent optimal controls to mean-field optimal controls is established in several settings, and graphon mean-field control frameworks (including on sparse graphs) have been developed recently. However, a unified theory describing how optimal control problems behave simultaneously under mean-field, graph-limit, and embedding limits, and which control-theoretic properties are preserved across all these procedures, has not been established and is widely cited as an open direction.

context_brief: Characterization of congruence lattices of SPS lattices
original_question: Which finite distributive lattices occur as congruence lattices of SPS lattices, where an SPS lattice is a finite slim planar semimodular lattice and 'slim' means that the lattice has no M3 sublattice? Equivalently, determine necessary and sufficient conditions for a finite distributive lattice D to be representable as Con L for some finite slim planar semimodular lattice L.
self_contained_problem:
A finite lattice $L$ is called semimodular if for all $a,b\in L$, whenever $a$ covers $a\wedge b$ then $a\vee b$ covers $b$. The lattice $L$ is called planar if it has a planar Hasse diagram, and slim if it contains no sublattice isomorphic to $M_3$ (the five-element modular nondistributive lattice with three atoms). An SPS lattice is a finite slim planar semimodular lattice.

For a finite lattice $L$, let $\operatorname{Con} L$ denote its congruence lattice; if $L$ is semimodular and finite then $\operatorname{Con} L$ is a finite distributive lattice.

Problem. Give necessary and sufficient conditions on a finite distributive lattice $D$ for there to exist an SPS lattice $L$ with $\operatorname{Con} L \cong D$. Equivalently, characterize the class of finite distributive lattices that arise as congruence lattices of finite slim planar semimodular lattices.
status_search_result: The problem is generally regarded as open. A growing list of necessary conditions on $\operatorname{Con} L$ for SPS lattices $L$ has been established (e.g., having at least two dual atoms when $|L|>2$; properties proved by G. Grätzer and G. Czédli; and infinitely many further properties via Czédli's "lamps"). However, no complete characterization (necessary and sufficient conditions) has been published as of recent work in 2023–2024.

original_question: In fixed-budget best arm identification, a bandit instance mu belongs to the class S of instances with a unique best arm, the learner uses exactly n samples, and then outputs an estimate I_hat_n of the best arm; the resulting error probability is p_{mu,n} = P_mu(I_hat_n != I*(mu)), where I*(mu) is the unique arm with the largest mean. Is there a natural algorithm class A and a well-defined instance-dependent function Gamma*_fb: S -> R such that every algorithm in A satisfies lim inf_{n->infinity} n / log(1/p_{mu,n}) >= Gamma*_fb(mu), while some algorithm in A also satisfies the matching upper bound lim sup_{n->infinity} n / log(1/p_{mu,n}) <= Gamma*_fb(mu), so that Gamma*_fb exactly characterizes the asymptotic complexity of the fixed-budget setting?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem with finitely many arms. A bandit instance $\mu = (\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_K)$ specifies the distribution of each arm; let $\mathcal{S}$ denote the class of instances admitting a unique best arm, i.e. a unique index $I^*(\mu) \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$ whose mean reward is strictly larger than that of every other arm.

In the fixed-budget best-arm identification problem, a total number of samples $n$ is fixed in advance. An algorithm consists of (i) a sampling rule that at each round $t = 1, \ldots, n$ chooses an arm $A_t$ as a (possibly randomized) function of past observations, and (ii) a decision rule that, after observing all $n$ samples, outputs a guess $\hat{I}_n \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ for the identity of the best arm. The error probability of the algorithm on instance $\mu$ with budget $n$ is
$$p_{\mu,n} := \mathbb{P}_\mu\bigl(\hat{I}_n \neq I^*(\mu)\bigr).$$

Question: Do there exist a class $\mathcal{A}$ of admissible algorithms and an instance-dependent function $\Gamma^*_{\mathrm{fb}} : \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item (lower bound) for every algorithm in $\mathcal{A}$ and every $\mu \in \mathcal{S}$,
$$\liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{n}{\log(1/p_{\mu,n})} \;\geq\; \Gamma^*_{\mathrm{fb}}(\mu),$$
\item (matching upper bound) there exists an algorithm in $\mathcal{A}$ such that for every $\mu \in \mathcal{S}$,
$$\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{n}{\log(1/p_{\mu,n})} \;\leq\; \Gamma^*_{\mathrm{fb}}(\mu),$$
\end{enumerate}
so that $\Gamma^*_{\mathrm{fb}}(\mu)$ exactly characterizes the asymptotic complexity of fixed-budget best-arm identification on $\mathcal{S}$?
status_search_result: The question is the well-known fixed-budget best-arm identification complexity problem posed by Qin (2022). Subsequent works (e.g., Degenne 2023 on the large-deviation perspective, and a 2026 reduction showing "fixed budget is no harder than fixed confidence up to logarithmic factors") have produced partial results, improved bounds, and structural connections to the fixed-confidence setting, but no work has provided a fully matching instance-dependent characterization $\Gamma^*_{\mathrm{fb}}$ together with a suitable algorithm class. The problem is widely cited as still open.

original_question: For two-armed Bernoulli bandits in the fixed-budget setting, Kaufmann et al. (2016) show that an optimal sampling vector exists, but that vector depends on the unknown means of the two arms and therefore is not available a priori. Is there an algorithm that can still achieve asymptotic optimality in this setting without requiring prior knowledge of those unknown arm means?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the fixed-budget best-arm identification problem for two-armed Bernoulli bandits. There are two arms with unknown means $\mu_1, \mu_2 \in (0,1)$, $\mu_1 \neq \mu_2$, and an algorithm is given a total budget of $T$ samples. At each round $t = 1, \dots, T$, the algorithm chooses an arm $A_t \in \{1,2\}$ (based on past observations) and observes an independent reward $X_t \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mu_{A_t})$. After $T$ rounds, the algorithm outputs a recommended arm $\hat{a}_T$, and its error probability is $p_T(\mu_1,\mu_2) = \Pr(\hat{a}_T \neq \arg\max_i \mu_i)$.

It is known that, for each instance $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$, there exists an optimal (instance-dependent) sampling proportion $w^*(\mu_1,\mu_2) \in (0,1)$ characterizing the best achievable asymptotic exponential decay rate
$$\Gamma^*(\mu_1,\mu_2) = -\lim_{T\to\infty} \tfrac{1}{T}\log p_T(\mu_1,\mu_2),$$
but $w^*$ depends on the unknown means.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm, not having prior knowledge of $\mu_1,\mu_2$, that is asymptotically optimal in the sense that
$$-\liminf_{T\to\infty} \tfrac{1}{T}\log p_T(\mu_1,\mu_2) \geq \Gamma^*(\mu_1,\mu_2)$$
for every instance $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$?
status_search_result: Subsequent work on universally optimal algorithms for A/B testing (Adusumilli, "On Universally Optimal Algorithms for A/B Testing," arXiv:2308.12000) addresses this question for two-armed Bernoulli bandits in fixed budget. It establishes that uniform sampling is universally asymptotically optimal: no algorithm in the natural class of consistent and stable algorithms can strictly outperform uniform sampling on any instance while matching it elsewhere. Thus uniform allocation—which requires no knowledge of the unknown means—achieves the asymptotic optimal rate for two-armed Bernoulli bandits.

context_brief: Tagged-leaf height in original interval model
original_question: In the original interval-splitting version of the critical beta-splitting model, where one follows a specified leaf i(n) rather than a uniformly random leaf, determine the distribution of the height of that leaf in both DTCS(n), the discrete-time tree built by recursive interval splitting, and CTCS(n), its continuous-time version in which a clade of size m splits after an Exponential(h_{m-1}) time.

Fix an integer $n\ge 2$ and consider the following interval-splitting construction of a random binary tree with $n$ leaves labelled $1,2,\dots,n$.

Discrete-time model DTCS(n). Start with the interval $[0,n]$, regarded as the root, containing the $n$ unit subintervals $[i-1,i]$, $i=1,\dots,n$, called "leaf-points." Recursively, any interval $[a,b]$ of integer length $m=b-a\ge 2$ that has not yet been split is split into two subintervals $[a,a+J]$ and $[a+J,b]$, where the split position $J\in\{1,2,\dots,m-1\}$ is chosen with the critical beta-splitting probabilities
$$q(m,j)=\frac{1}{h_{m-1}}\Big(\frac{1}{j}+\frac{1}{m-j}\Big)\cdot\frac{1}{2},\qquad j=1,\dots,m-1,$$
where $h_{k}=\sum_{r=1}^{k}1/r$ is the $k$-th harmonic number. (Equivalently, $q(m,j)=\frac{1}{h_{m-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{j(m-j)}\cdot\frac{m}{2}$ after symmetrisation.) The recursion stops when every remaining interval has length $1$; these unit intervals are the leaves and inherit the labels $1,\dots,n$ from their positions. The resulting rooted binary tree is DTCS(n), and the height of a leaf is the number of edges on the path from the root to that leaf.

The same recursive splitting is performed, but each unsplit interval of integer length $m\ge 2$ waits an independent $\mathrm{Exponential}(h_{m-1})$ time before splitting (with split position again distributed as $q(m,\cdot)$). The height of a leaf in CTCS(n) is the total continuous time elapsed from the root split down to that leaf.

Consider the Markov chain on the integers $\{1,2,3,\ldots\}$ called the harmonic descent chain, defined as follows. For $n\ge 2$, let $h_{n-1}=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}1/j$. From state $n\ge 2$, the chain jumps to state $i\in\{1,2,\ldots,n-1\}$ with probability
$$p(n,i)=\frac{1}{h_{n-1}}\cdot\frac{1}{n-i},\qquad 1\le i\le n-1,$$
and state $1$ is absorbing. For integers $n\ge m\ge 1$, define
$$a(n,m)=\Pr\big(\text{the chain started at } n \text{ ever visits state } m\big),$$
with the convention $a(n,n)=1$. It is known that the limit
$$a(m)=\lim_{n\to\infty} a(n,m)$$
exists for every $m\ge 1$.

(a) Find explicit (quantitative) bounds for $|a(n,m)-a(m)|$ as $n\to\infty$ with $m$ fixed (and, more generally, jointly in $n$ and $m$).

(b) Prove the following Ansatz. Let $f:\{2,3,\ldots\}\to[0,\infty)$ satisfy $f(j)=O(j^k)$ for some $k\ge 0$.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] If $\sum_{j\ge 2} a(j)f(j)<\infty$, then 
$$\sum_{j=2}^n a(n,j)f(j)\ \longrightarrow\ \sum_{j\ge 2} a(j)f(j)\quad\text{as } n\to\infty.$$
\item[(ii)] If $\sum_{j\ge 2} a(j)f(j)=\infty$, then 
$$\sum_{j=2}^n a(n,j)f(j)\ \sim\ \sum_{j=2}^n a(j)f(j)\quad\text{as } n\to\infty.$$
\end{itemize}

Background and setup.

For each integer n ≥ 2, the discrete-time critical beta-splitting tree DTCS(n) is the random rooted combinatorial tree on n labeled leaves defined recursively as follows. Start from a root carrying the leaf-set {1,…,n}. A cluster of m ≥ 2 leaves is split into two child clusters of sizes i and m−i (1 ≤ i ≤ m−1) with probability
  q_m(i) = (1/h_{m−1}) · 1/(i(m−i)),  where h_{m−1} = Σ_{j=1}^{m−1} 1/j,
independently for distinct clusters, until every cluster has size 1 (a leaf). The resulting finite rooted tree, with its labeled leaves, is DTCS(n).

It is known that the local weak limit, as n → ∞, of the random sequence (T_i^{(n)}, i = 1, …, n) exists and is a stationary process (T_i, i ∈ ℤ) taking values in an appropriate space of rooted locally finite trees; call this the stationary fringe process.

Let Φ be a measurable real-valued functional on the tree-space such that Φ(T_i^{(n)}) and Φ(T_i) are well-defined.

Question.

Suppose that Φ satisfies a central limit theorem along the stationary fringe process, in the sense that there exist constants μ ∈ ℝ and σ > 0 such that
  (1/√m) · ( Σ_{i=0}^{m−1} Φ(T_i) − m μ )  ⇒  𝒩(0, σ^2)  as m → ∞.

Does it then follow that the analogous central limit theorem holds for DTCS(n), namely
  (1/√n) · ( Σ_{i=1}^{n} Φ(T_i^{(n)}) − n μ )  ⇒  𝒩(0, σ^2)  as n → ∞?

Determine whether this implication is true for every such functional Φ, or exhibit a Φ for which the fringe-process CLT holds but the DTCS(n) CLT fails.

paper_title: The Critical Beta-splitting Random Tree II: Overview and Open Problems
context_brief: Hidden symmetry in the growth process
original_question: In the n→∞ inductive growth picture for CTCS(n), let p↑ be the limiting probability that a new leaf is added by branch extension and let p↗ be the limiting probability of a side-bud extension. Explain whether the observed identity p↑ = p↗ can be derived from an underlying symmetry of the tree shape or the growth dynamics.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the critical beta-splitting random tree model defined as follows. For an integer m ≥ 2, a clade of m leaves is recursively partitioned into two sub-clades of sizes i and m−i (1 ≤ i ≤ m−1) with probability proportional to 1/(i(m−i)); recursion stops at clades of size 1. This produces a random rooted binary tree CTCS(n) on n labeled leaves. The family {CTCS(n) : n ≥ 2} is consistent under the operation "delete a uniformly random leaf and contract the resulting degree-2 vertex," and therefore admits an inductive growth construction: CTCS(n+1) is obtained from CTCS(n) by inserting one new leaf according to a prescribed conditional distribution.

In this growth construction, classify the insertion of the new leaf into one of three local types:
 • branch extension: the new leaf is attached so that one bud of an existing terminal cherry is replaced by a new branch ending in a pair of buds;
 • side-bud addition: the new leaf is attached as a side-bud in the interior of an existing edge;
 • side-bud extension: an existing side-bud is replaced by a new branch with two terminal buds.

Let p↑, p→, and p↗ denote, respectively, the limiting (as n → ∞) probabilities of these three event types at the step from CTCS(n) to CTCS(n+1). It is observed that p↑ = p↗.

Determine whether the identity p↑ = p↗ can be derived as a consequence of some intrinsic symmetry of the random tree shape or of the growth dynamics, and if so exhibit such a symmetry.
status_search_result: The question appears as an open problem in the overview of the critical beta-splitting random tree model (2023). Subsequent papers in the series (2024–2025) on the exchangeable partition representation, fringe tree, leaf-height Mellin analysis, and contraction methods extend the theory but do not announce a resolution of this particular identity via symmetry. No search result indicates that p↑ = p↗ has been explained by an established symmetry of the tree shape or the growth dynamics.

paper_title: Seven open problems in applied combinatorics
original_question: Let G=(V,E,ω) be a weighted simple graph. Construct an algorithm that computes an ε-net L⊂V for G and simultaneously improves on the existing ε-net algorithms by using fewer landmarks and running in less time than the currently available methods.
self_contained_problem:
Let G = (V, E, ω) be a weighted simple connected graph with edge-weight function ω : E → ℝ_{>0}, inducing the shortest-path (geodesic) metric d_G on V. For ε > 0, a subset L ⊆ V is called an ε-net of G if:
(a) for every v ∈ V there exists ℓ ∈ L with d_G(v, ℓ) ≤ ε (covering), and
(b) for any two distinct ℓ, ℓ' ∈ L one has d_G(ℓ, ℓ') > ε (packing/separation).
Elements of L are called landmarks.

Three known procedures for constructing such an ε-net are:
(i) a greedy algorithm that repeatedly selects a vertex at distance > ε from the current set of landmarks;
(ii) an iterative algorithm that updates landmarks via local exchanges;
(iii) an SPT-pruning algorithm based on pruning shortest-path trees.

Design an algorithm A that, given any input (G, ε), outputs an ε-net L ⊆ V of G and simultaneously satisfies both of the following:
(1) The cardinality |L| produced by A is, in the worst case (and/or on benchmark instances on which the three algorithms above have been compared), strictly smaller than the cardinality produced by each of the greedy, iterative, and SPT-pruning algorithms.
(2) The running time of A is strictly smaller than that of each of the greedy, iterative, and SPT-pruning algorithms.

Equivalently: provide an ε-net construction that strictly improves both the landmark count and the running time of all previously known ε-net algorithms for weighted simple graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists.
status_search_result: The problem is stated as an open problem in a 2023 list of seven open problems in applied combinatorics. A targeted web search did not surface any subsequent paper or preprint claiming an ε-net algorithm for weighted simple graphs that simultaneously beats the greedy, iterative, and SPT-pruning algorithms in both landmark count and running time. The status therefore appears to remain open.
